endorsements.quote: Researchers should make responsible use of AI; use standardized reporting guidelines [ 58 ]; systematically compare different types of AI-based tools; evaluate the accuracy, repeatability, and reproducibility of the tools; and incorporate ethical and legal considerations.

The false myth paradigm tests the AI’s ability to reject outdated concepts or information and content not substantiated by scientific evidence, whereas the challenging question paradigm assesses how AI handles nuanced medical issues.

The expert consensus paradigm involves a panel of medical experts evaluating AI-generated diagnoses and treatment plans, whereas the cross-discipline validation paradigm cross-checks AI insights with those of professionals from different medical fields, ensuring comprehensive evaluation.
In particular, the algorithm transparency and audit paradigm plays a crucial role here, ensuring that AI’s reasoning is accessible and understandable to clinicians.
AI in this context is a tool that augments but does not replace the clinician’s judgment.

unlisted_practices: Regularly review AI recommendations through ethics committee or legal team review rounds to ensure adherence to ethical guidelines and legal standards.
Continuously update AI systems through a feedback loop using clinician feedback and real-world outcomes so they remain aligned with current medical evidence.
Engage a broad range of stakeholders, including patients, clinicians, ethicists, and legal experts, throughout AI evaluation.
Apply a layered, sequential combination of verification paradigms, prioritized by clinical context, to evaluate generative AI.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual framework paper proposing 11 verification paradigms and guidelines for responsible clinical generative AI rather than an empirical study.
